In 1986, Rumelhart et al. applied the back propagation (BP) algorithm to the training process of the multilayer perceptron, enabling neural networks to automatically adjust weight parameters through gradient descent, which significantly advanced the development of neural networks in the field of machine learning [55].
212: A BP network is usually composed of an input layer, hidden layers and an output layer. However, when the number of network layers is large, the BP algorithm is prone to problems such as vanishing or exploding gradients, which affects model training performance. To overcome the limitations of traditional neural networks in image processing tasks, LeCun et al. proposed the convolutional neural network (CNN). 214: from the biological visual system, and through local connectivity and weight-sharing mechanisms significantly reduces the number of model parameters while improving feature extraction capability [56].
215: Compared with traditional fully connected networks, CNNs can more efficiently capture local structural information in images, such as edges, textures and shapes, and are therefore widely applied in the field of computer vision. In addition, He et al. proposed the residual network (ResNet), alleviating the degradation problem in training deep networks through residual connections [57]. Kim et al. proposed the deeply-recursive convolutional network (DRCN), using a recursive structure to enlarge the receptive field and enhance feature representation [58]. Huang et al. proposed DenseNet, strengthening feature reuse and gradient propagation through dense connections [59]. Tong et al. introduced dense skip connections into the image super-resolution task, proposing SRDenseNet to improve the reconstruction capability for high-frequency detail [60].

This process simulates the human visual system's mechanism of attending to local regions, allowing the model to focus on important information regions in the image. Multiple convolutional layers are stacked one after another in a hierarchical structure, thereby progressively completing the extraction process from shallow features to deep features.
224: In the shallow stages of the network, convolutional layers mainly capture low-level features in the image, such as colour variation and texture structure; as network depth increases, convolutional layers gradually learn higher-level abstract features, such as the shape and semantic information of targets. Each convolutional layer is usually composed of multiple convolution kernels; a common kernel size is 3x3, which effectively reduces the number of parameters while guaranteeing representational capability, and is therefore widely used.

Here, Q represents the word currently requiring attention, K represents the positional features of each word in the sequence, and V contains the specific semantic information. All three vectors are obtained from the input data through linear transformation. Finally, the computational form of self-attention is as follows:

Finally, the normalised result is multiplied with V, thereby obtaining an output representation containing contextual information. On this basis, the Transformer further introduces the multi-head attention mechanism, which computes attention results in parallel across multiple subspaces, captures the relationships between features from different perspectives, and finally concatenates and fuses them to form the final output of the Transformer module.
263: Following the Transformer's success in natural language processing, Dosovitskiy et al. proposed the Vision Transformer (ViT) model in 2020 [50], extending this structure to computer vision tasks such as image classification and semantic segmentation, and achieving performance comparable to mainstream convolutional neural networks. Thereafter, the Transformer gradually became one of the important research directions in the visual field, demonstrating potential superior to traditional CNN models in multiple tasks. Unlike convolutional neural networks, which rely on local receptive fields, the Vision Transformer can directly establish global relationships among input features through the self-attention mechanism, thereby characterising the contextual information of the image more comprehensively. This globally-modelled approach gives the model stronger representational capability when processing complex scenes.
264: In terms of specific implementation, the Transformer generally adopts a multi-head self-attention mechanism, mapping input features into multiple subspaces for parallel computation so as to obtain attention distributions under different dimensions. The computation results of the various subspaces are subsequently concatenated and fused, thereby improving the model's capability to characterise feature relationships. In addition, because self-attention itself has no capability to perceive positional information, positional encoding must be additionally introduced to supplement the spatial or ordinal information in the sequence.
265: Although the Transformer possesses good modelling capability, the computational complexity of its self-attention grows quadratically with the length of the input sequence. When the sequence length is L, the computational complexity of multi-head self-attention is O(N . L2 d), where d denotes the feature dimension. This computational characteristic entails considerable resource consumption when processing high-resolution images. To alleviate this problem, Dosovitskiy et al. proposed dividing the image into multiple patches as input, thereby reducing the computational scale. However, in high-resolution tasks requiring fine-grained modelling, this method still has certain limitations.    2.1.3 The Mamba Model

280: 2.2 Theoretical Analysis of Underwater Image Super-Resolution
282: In the underwater environment, the process of light propagation is jointly affected by absorption effects and scattering effects; these two factors are the main causes of the decline in underwater image quality. The absorption effect refers to the fact that when light propagates through a body of water, part of its energy is absorbed by water molecules and by substances dissolved in the water, causing the light intensity to gradually attenuate. Because light of different wavelengths is absorbed at different rates in water - for example, blue light attenuates relatively slowly - underwater images generally exhibit a pronounced blue-green colour cast. The scattering effect occurs when light encounters suspended particles or other minute substances in the water during propagation, causing its direction of propagation to change and thereby producing phenomena such as blurring or brightness variation in the image. The Jaffe-McGlamery underwater imaging model is shown in Figure 2.11. According to the direction of scattering, it can be divided into two forms: forward scattering and backward scattering. Forward scattering changes the propagation path of light, making image edges blurred, while backward scattering reflects part of the light back to the camera equipment, producing a halo effect and reducing image clarity. Taking both light absorption and scattering into comprehensive consideration, the underwater image degradation process can generally be described by the classical underwater imaging model, whose mathematical expression is as follows:

290: 2.2.2 Principles of Underwater Image Super-Resolution Reconstruction
291: During acquisition, underwater images often suffer from problems such as low resolution, missing detail and insufficient texture information; it is therefore necessary to reconstruct the image through super-resolution technology in order to obtain higher-quality visual information. Super-resolution reconstruction refers to the process of recovering a high-resolution image from a low-resolution image through an algorithm; its core objective is to reconstruct the high-frequency detail information in the image so that it appears visually clearer. At present, image super-resolution reconstruction methods are mainly divided into traditional interpolation methods and deep-learning-based methods. Throughout the development of image super-resolution technology, interpolation-based methods have consistently held an important position. Their core idea is to estimate and fill in unknown pixel values between known pixel points through mathematical interpolation, thereby achieving an increase in image resolution.
293: Bilinear interpolation is a method of interpolating in two-dimensional space, computing the value of the target pixel by performing linear interpolation separately in two directions. Specifically, for a pixel requiring interpolation, bilinear interpolation first considers the four neighbouring pixels around that pixel. It then performs one linear interpolation in the horizontal direction on each of the two pairs of adjacent pixels, and subsequently performs one linear interpolation in the vertical direction on the two interpolation results obtained, thereby obtaining the interpolation result for the target pixel.

306: Deconvolution is a distinctive form of convolution used to predict the corresponding high-resolution image from low-resolution image feature maps [62]. The specific operational process is as follows: it begins with edge padding to proportionally enlarge the feature map size, and then performs a convolution operation with a convolution kernel and stride of appropriate size, so as to produce an HR image of the expected dimensions. Deconvolution upsampling combines the characteristics of traditional convolution with the advantages of end-to-end image reconstruction, and has been widely applied in the field of image super-resolution. However, if the convolution kernel size and stride are not proportional, non-uniform aliasing phenomena may arise in the generated image.

By minimising this loss function, the model parameters can be continually optimised so that the predicted image gradually approaches the true image.
324: During training, the back-propagation algorithm is generally used to compute the gradient of the loss function with respect to the model parameters, and an optimisation algorithm is used to update the parameters theta. The model parameter update process usually begins from random initialisation, and through continuous iterative adjustment of the parameters the loss function is gradually reduced. When the model's performance on the validation set stabilises - that is, when the loss value no longer decreases significantly - the training process can end. Among the many optimisation algorithms, the Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation) optimiser is widely applied in deep learning model training. This method adaptively adjusts the learning rate of each parameter by combining first-moment and second-moment estimates of the gradient, thereby improving training stability while guaranteeing convergence speed. 329: Object detection is one of the important research directions in the field of computer vision. Its main task is to locate and identify targets of interest in an image - that is, to accomplish both "classification" and "localisation" simultaneously. Unlike traditional image classification, which outputs only a category label, object detection must output both the position and the category information of targets, and therefore has higher complexity.

335: Two-stage detectors generally first generate region proposals and then perform classification and regression prediction on the candidate regions; the structure diagram is shown in Figure 2.17. Typical representatives include models such as R-CNN, Fast R-CNN and Faster R-CNN.
336: R-CNN first generates candidate regions through selective search, then uses a convolutional neural network to extract features and perform classification. However, this method suffers from relatively low computational efficiency. To address this, Fast R-CNN significantly improved detection speed by sharing convolutional feature maps, while Faster R-CNN further introduced the Region Proposal Network (RPN) to achieve end-to-end learning of candidate regions, thereby substantially improving detection efficiency and accuracy. The main advantage of two-stage methods is their relatively high detection accuracy, making them especially suitable for tasks with high detection-accuracy requirements. Their disadvantage, however, is high computational complexity, making it difficult to meet real-time requirements.

340: Unlike two-stage methods, one-stage detectors unify the target localisation and classification processes within a single network, thereby significantly increasing detection speed; the structure diagram is shown in Figure 2.18. Representative models include the YOLO (You Only Look Once) series and SSD (Single Shot MultiBox Detector). The YOLO model divides the input image into multiple grid cells and directly predicts the target category and bounding box information within each cell, thereby achieving end-to-end detection. Its objective function generally consists of localisation error, classification error and confidence error. Through successive version iterations (such as YOLOv3, YOLOv5 and YOLOv8), the model has achieved a good balance between accuracy and speed.
341: The SSD model, by performing detection on multi-scale feature maps, improves recognition capability for targets of different sizes. Compared with YOLO, SSD performs more stably in small-target detection.
342: The advantage of one-stage methods lies in their fast detection speed, making them suitable for real-time detection scenarios such as autonomous driving and video surveillance. However, their detection accuracy is generally slightly lower than that of two-stage methods.

345: 2.3.3 Key Technologies of Deep-Learning-Based Object Detection
346: With the development of deep learning, object detection technology has continued to evolve, forming a series of key technologies. (1) Feature extraction network: object detection models generally rely on a convolutional neural network as the feature extraction backbone - for example structures such as VGG and ResNet - extracting multi-scale features of the image through multi-layer convolution.
347: (2) Multi-scale feature fusion: because the scale of targets in an image varies considerably, modern detection algorithms generally adopt a feature pyramid network (FPN) structure for multi-scale feature fusion, thereby improving the model's detection capability for targets of different sizes.
348: (3) Anchor mechanism: the anchor mechanism presets candidate boxes of different sizes and aspect ratios so that the model can predict target positions more efficiently. However, this method requires manual design of parameters and has relatively low flexibility. (4) Anchor-free detection: in recent years, anchor-free methods have gradually risen to prominence; by directly predicting key points or centre-point positions they avoid complex anchor-box design and improve the model's generalisation capability. (5) Loss function design: object detection tasks generally adopt a multi-task loss function, including classification loss and regression loss. For example, the regression loss may use L1 loss or GIoU loss to improve bounding-box prediction accuracy.    2.3.4 Analysis of the Characteristics of Underwater Object Detection
349: Compared with ordinary scenes, the underwater environment has characteristics such as illumination attenuation, colour distortion and noise interference, and these factors have a significant impact on object detection performance. Therefore, in underwater object detection tasks it is necessary to combine image enhancement with feature extraction methods to improve the model's adaptability to complex environments.
350: At the same time, because underwater targets are often small in scale with blurred boundaries, traditional detection models are prone to missed detections or false detections. Therefore, combining super-resolution reconstruction with deep feature modelling methods can effectively improve detection performance, which is also the key direction of the subsequent research in this thesis.
352: This chapter has discussed the related theoretical foundations of underwater image processing and object detection tasks. First, the underwater image degradation model was analysed, explaining the main causes of declining underwater image quality from the two aspects of light absorption and scattering, and describing the degradation process mathematically through an imaging model.
353: Subsequently, the basic principles of underwater image super-resolution reconstruction were introduced, with particular focus on the application of convolutional neural networks in image reconstruction tasks, and a detailed explanation of the model structure, training process and optimisation methods. In the deep learning theory section, the basic structure and working mechanism of convolutional neural networks were systematically expounded; at the same time, the Transformer model and its self-attention mechanism were analysed, and the advantages of the Mamba model in long-sequence modelling were further introduced.
355: Finally, the basic principles and mainstream methods of object detection were summarised, including the characteristics and applicable scenarios of two-stage and one-stage
356: detection algorithms, and the challenges facing object detection were analysed in the light of the characteristics of the underwater environment. The content of this chapter provides an important theoretical foundation for the design of the subsequent underwater image enhancement and object detection algorithms.
